_readme: Verified survivors a month's editor did not use, each tagged with the month it fits, routed forward rather than thrown away. The Makers' carry delivered 29 pre-verified entries by December. Appended by land-month.js from month.json's `unused`; read by prep-month.js into the next month's brief. Never edited by hand.

entries.quote: And, when you want something, all the universe conspires in helping you to achieve it.
entries.source: Paulo Coelho, The Alchemist, Part One (Melchizedek, the king of Salem) (trans. Alan R. Clarke, 1993)
entries.note: Verified in Clarke’s translation with the leading And; Melchizedek speaks it. Hope rather than beginning.

entries.quote: Light, my light, the world-filling light, the eye-kissing light, heart-sweetening light!
entries.source: Rabindranath Tagore, Gitanjali (Song Offerings), poem 57, first line (trans. the author, 1912)
entries.note: Verified in Tagore’s own English of 1912. A light line for the dark month.

entries.quote: One cannot think well, love well, sleep well, if one has not dined well.
entries.source: Virginia Woolf, A Room of One’s Own, ch. 1 (1929)
entries.note: Verified. Woolf’s other survivor, the opening of Mrs Dalloway, is the stronger January line, and neither made the month; one person per month either way.

entries.quote: Ships at a distance have every man’s wish on board.
entries.source: Zora Neale Hurston, Their Eyes Were Watching God, chapter 1, the opening sentence (1937)
entries.note: Verified opening line. The paragraph goes on to say some ships never land, so it is hopeful only as a single sentence; place it with that in mind.

entries.quote: Another heavenly day.
entries.source: Samuel Beckett, Happy Days, Act I, Winnie’s first words after the bell (Grove Press, 1961) (Winnie)
entries.note: Verified opening line, but it is the ironic optimism of a woman buried to the waist, and a VERIFIED line may carry no note. Place it only where the source line can carry the context.

entries.quote: If more of us valued food and cheer and song above hoarded gold, it would be a merrier world.
entries.source: J. R. R. Tolkien, The Hobbit, chapter 18, The Return Journey (George Allen and Unwin, 1937) (Thorin Oakenshield)
entries.note: Verified in Thorin’s farewell; the real text behind Calendar For Life candidate 511. A gratitude line.

entries.quote: Mankind was my business. The common welfare was my business; charity, mercy, forbearance, and benevolence, were, all, my business.
entries.source: Charles Dickens, A Christmas Carol, Stave One (Jacob Marley’s Ghost)
entries.note: Verified in Stave One with the first-edition commas. A December line by its book.

entries.quote: You must sit down, sayes Love, and taste my meat: / So I did sit and eat.
entries.source: George Herbert, Love (III), lines 17 to 18, The Temple (Cambridge, 1633)
entries.note: Verified in two copies of the 1633 printing, closing couplet of the last poem of The Church. A gratitude line.

entries.quote: Somebody loves us all.
entries.source: Elizabeth Bishop, Filling Station, closing line, Questions of Travel (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1965)
entries.note: Verified, the closing line of the poem; four words, a very bare card. A gratitude line.

entries.quote: I have finished a monument more lasting than bronze and loftier than the Pyramids’ royal pile, one that no wasting rain, no furious north wind can destroy, or the countless chain of years and the ages’ flight.
entries.source: Horace, Odes, Book III, ode 30, lines 1 to 5 (trans. C. E. Bennett, Loeb Classical Library, 1914)
entries.note: Verified in Bennett’s 1914 Loeb, p. 279, unchanged by the 1927 revision. Horace landed in March with the Epistle to Lollius. The work that outlasts its maker: November.

entries.quote: But I maintain that she would come if we worked for her, and that so to work, even in poverty and obscurity, is worth while.
entries.source: Virginia Woolf, A Room of One’s Own, chapter 6, the closing sentence (1929)
entries.note: CORRECTED: a note names her. She is Shakespeare’s sister, the gifted poet Woolf imagines, who died young and never wrote a word. The closing sentence of the book, so December’s by right.

entries.quote: But all things excellent are as difficult as they are rare.
entries.source: Baruch Spinoza, Ethics, Part V, Proposition 42, Scholium, the closing sentence (trans. R. H. M. Elwes, 1883)
entries.note: Verified closing line of the Ethics in Elwes. Carried to March as a discipline line and not used: it merely fits there, and as a closing sentence it belongs to December.

entries.quote: All the same I’m not going to accept your kind invitation, for the time being at any rate. The reason is that my pink cactus is probably going to flower. It’s a very rare plant I’ve been given, and I’m told that in our climate it flowers only once every four years.
entries.source: Colette, Break of Day, the letter that opens the book, pp. 5 to 6 (Sido, the narrator’s mother) (trans. Enid McLeod, 1961)
entries.note: CORRECTED and re-verified: a comma after All the same restored. The printed page is lending restricted, so the punctuation is medium confidence. A flowering that is worth waiting for, which is hope more than renewal.

entries.quote: Life is occupied in both perpetuating itself and in surpassing itself; if all it does is maintain itself, then living is only not dying, and human existence is indistinguishable from an absurd vegetation; a life justifies itself only if its effort to perpetuate itself is integrated into its surpassing and if this surpassing has no other limits than those which the subject assigns himself.
entries.source: Simone de Beauvoir, The Ethics of Ambiguity, Part III, 2, Freedom and Liberation (trans. Bernard Frechtman, 1948)
entries.note: Verified. Long, and it argues rather than opens the day; it belongs with the month on living and dying.

entries.quote: To awaken quite alone in a strange town is one of the pleasantest sensations in the world. You are surrounded by adventure. You have no idea of what is in store for you, but you will, if you are wise and know the art of travel, let yourself go on the stream of the unknown and accept whatever comes in the spirit in which the gods may offer it.
entries.source: Freya Stark, Baghdad Sketches, In the Moslem Quarter, opening sentences, p. 17 (John Murray, 1937)
entries.note: Verified, and a waking line, which April already had four of. Held for the month of hope.

entries.quote: May lily-dotted lakes delight your eye; / May shade-trees bid the heat of noonday cease; / May soft winds blow the lotus-pollen nigh; / May all your path be pleasantness and peace.
entries.source: Kālidāsa, Shakuntala, Act IV (Invisible beings) (trans. Arthur W. Ryder, 1912)
entries.note: Verified to the letter, and dropped on rule 2 alone: the refuter could find no standard reference entry for the stanza, and Shakuntala is not known by it. A blessing on someone setting out, so it is offered again in December.

entries.quote: The world stands out on either side / No wider than the heart is wide; / Above the world is stretched the sky,— / No higher than the soul is high.
entries.source: Edna St. Vincent Millay, Renascence, lines 203 to 206, Renascence and Other Poems (Mitchell Kennerley, 1917)
entries.note: Verified. A poem of being born again, kept whole for the month that is named for it.

entries.quote: And the miraculous comes so close / to the ruined, dirty houses— / something not known to anyone at all, / but wild in our breast for centuries.
entries.source: Anna Akhmatova, ‘Everything is plundered’, lines 9 to 12, Anno Domini MCMXXI (trans. Stanley Kunitz with Max Hayward, 1973)
entries.note: Verified at medium confidence. Another Akhmatova is already held for October, so this one goes to December.

entries.quote: I got out of bed / on two strong legs. / It might have been / otherwise. I ate / cereal, sweet / milk, ripe, flawless / peach. It might / have been otherwise.
entries.source: Jane Kenyon, Otherwise, lines 1 to 8, Otherwise: New and Selected Poems (Graywolf Press, 1996)
entries.note: Verified. A gratitude line and a mortality line at once, so it belongs to November.

entries.quote: You do not have to be good. / You do not have to walk on your knees / for a hundred miles through the desert repenting. / You only have to let the soft animal of your body / love what it loves.
entries.source: Mary Oliver, Wild Geese, lines 1 to 5, Dream Work (Atlantic Monthly Press, 1986), p. 14
entries.note: Verified against reprints crediting Dream Work, no comma before repenting. April landed eight poems and this one is about permission rather than the road.

entries.quote: And we should consider every day lost on which we have not danced at least once.
entries.source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Thus Spoke Zarathustra, Third Part, On Old and New Tablets, 23 (Zarathustra) (trans. Walter Kaufmann, 1954)
entries.note: Verified in Kaufmann, The Portable Nietzsche, p. 322. Nietzsche stands at two of three and his child at play is also held, so only one of the two can ever land; this is the better of them.

entries.quote: Give me Books, fruit, French wine and fine weather and a little music out of doors, played by somebody I do not know.
entries.source: John Keats, Letters, to Fanny Keats, Winchester, 28 August 1819 (ed. Sidney Colvin, 1891), p. 285
entries.note: Verified letter. Held: a list of things to be glad of, which is a thanksgiving rather than a maxim.

entries.quote: It’s been my experience that you can nearly always enjoy things if you make up your mind firmly that you will.
entries.source: L. M. Montgomery, Anne of Green Gables, ch. V, Anne’s History (Anne Shirley, to Marilla Cuthbert)
entries.note: Verified. Held: Anne on making up your mind to enjoy things reads as gratitude before it reads as counsel.

entries.quote: In seed time learn, in harvest teach, in winter enjoy.
entries.source: William Blake, The Marriage of Heaven and Hell, Proverbs of Hell, the first proverb, plate 7 (1790)
entries.note: Corrected the spelling: Blake engraved In seed time as two words. Held: the proverb ends in winter enjoy, which is a thanksgiving.

entries.quote: You do not have to be good.
entries.source: Mary Oliver, Wild Geese, the opening line, Dream Work (Atlantic Monthly Press, 1986)
entries.note: Verified opening line. Held: you do not have to be good is a door opening, which is December’s promise.

entries.quote: I got out of bed / on two strong legs. / It might have been / otherwise.
entries.source: Jane Kenyon, Otherwise, lines 1 to 4, the fourth cut at its full stop, Otherwise: New and Selected Poems (Graywolf, 1996)
entries.note: Corrected the locator: the quotation stops at the poem’s own full stop inside the fourth line. Held: it might have been otherwise is gratitude and mortality together.

entries.quote: Now I become myself.
entries.source: May Sarton, Now I Become Myself, line 1, first sentence only, Collected Poems 1930 to 1993 (W. W. Norton, 1993)
entries.note: Corrected the locator and the edition, both at medium confidence. Held: now I become myself is a beginning, so December.

entries.quote: A classic is a book that has never finished saying what it has to say.
entries.source: Italo Calvino, Why Read the Classics?, definition 6 (trans. Patrick Creagh, 1986)
entries.note: Verified. Held again: a book that has never finished saying what it has to say is the promise December keeps.

entries.quote: The maturity of man—that means, to have reacquired the seriousness that one had as a child at play.
entries.source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Beyond Good and Evil, chapter IV, Apophthegms and Interludes, section 94 (trans. Helen Zimmern, 1907)
entries.note: Corrected: Zimmern’s translation is 1907. Held: the seriousness of a child at play is a renewal, and Nietzsche stands at two of three.

entries.quote: But then I have always supposed it to be my own fault—because I would not take the trouble of practising.
entries.source: Jane Austen, Pride and Prejudice, ch. 31: vol. II, ch. 8 in the 1813 edition (Elizabeth Bennet, to Mr Darcy)
entries.note: Verified against the first edition of 1813. Held: Elizabeth on not taking the trouble of practising is a rueful thanks for what she did not do.

entries.quote: A little madness in the Spring / Is wholesome even for the King, / But God be with the Clown, / Who ponders this tremendous scene— / This whole experiment of green, / As if it were his own!
entries.source: Emily Dickinson, ‘A little madness in the Spring’, The Single Hound, poem XXXVIII (Little, Brown, 1914)
entries.note: Corrected: the poem is number XXXVIII in The Single Hound. Held: a little madness in the Spring is renewal, and Dickinson stands at two of three.

entries.quote: I was always embarrassed by the words sacred, glorious, and sacrifice and the expression in vain.
entries.source: Ernest Hemingway, A Farewell to Arms, Book III, chapter 27 (Frederic Henry) (Charles Scribner’s Sons, 1929)
entries.note: Verified in the Scribner text of 1929 and attacked without a mark on it. Held only because one Hemingway can stand in a month and two are already carried.

entries.quote: To think is to forget differences, generalize, make abstractions.
entries.source: Jorge Luis Borges, Funes the Memorious, in Labyrinths, closing pages (trans. James E. Irby, 1962)
entries.note: Verified in Irby’s Labyrinths after a refutation sent it back. The Kerrigan wording is a different rendering of the same close.

entries.quote: We are learning that a standard of social ethics is not attained by travelling a sequestered byway, but by mixing on the thronged and common road where all must turn out for one another, and at least see the size of one another’s burdens.
entries.source: Jane Addams, Democracy and Social Ethics, chapter I, Introduction (Macmillan, 1902)
entries.note: Verified in the Introduction of 1902. Seeing the size of one another’s burdens, which is sympathy more than clarity.

entries.quote: Untruth naturally afflicts historical information.
entries.source: Ibn Khaldun, The Muqaddimah, the opening of Book One of the Kitab al-Ibar (trans. Franz Rosenthal, 1958)
entries.note: Corrected to the opening of Book One of the Kitab al Ibar after a refutation showed Rosenthal keeps the Introduction apart. No page is printed because none was opened.

entries.quote: The problem in public life is learning to overcome terror; the problem in married life is learning to overcome boredom.
entries.source: Gabriel García Márquez, Love in the Time of Cholera, chapter 4 (Fermina Daza) (trans. Edith Grossman, 1988)
entries.note: Corrected: the sentence is Fermina Daza’s own. Held: it is plain speech about two kinds of life rather than counsel.

entries.quote: He who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that.
entries.source: John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, chapter II, Of the Liberty of Thought and Discussion (1859)
entries.note: Verified. Held: knowing both sides is the discipline of clear seeing, which is June’s ground.

entries.quote: I can resist everything except temptation.
entries.source: Oscar Wilde, Lady Windermere’s Fan, First Act (Lord Darlington)
entries.note: Verified, First Act. Held: the inversion is wit about self-knowledge and the play rebukes it in the next line.

entries.quote: That which does not kill me, makes me stronger.
entries.source: Friedrich Nietzsche, The Twilight of the Idols, Maxims and Missiles, 8 (trans. Anthony M. Ludovici, 1911)
entries.note: Verified. Held: the most abused sentence in the trade, and at six in the morning it is harder than the month needs.

entries.quote: In every town and every village and every mud hut in the world there is always a man who loves children and who will fight to make a good world for them.
entries.source: Lillian Hellman, Watch on the Rhine, Act Three, his farewell to his children (Kurt Müller) (Random House, 1941)
entries.note: Corrected wording: the printed play carries the longer form with the three and joined clauses, not the 1943 film version. Held: the Drama lane took three.

entries.quote: The fairest action of our human life, / Is scorning to revenge an injury: / For who forgives without a further strife, / His adversary’s heart to him doth tie.
entries.source: Elizabeth Cary, The Tragedy of Mariam, the close of Act 4, lines 1 to 4 (Chorus) (1613 quarto)
entries.note: Corrected: the spelling is modernised from the 1613 quarto but the pointing is the quarto pointing, comma in line 1 and colon in line 2. Held: forbearance rather than endurance.

entries.quote: For I’se still goin’, honey, / I’se still climbin’, / And life for me ain’t been no crystal stair.
entries.source: Langston Hughes, Mother to Son, the closing three lines, The Crisis, December 1922 (the mother)
entries.note: Verified. Held: the Poetry lane was full and Mother to Son wants a month that can give it the whole stair.

entries.quote: For there is no friend like a sister / In calm or stormy weather; / To cheer one on the tedious way, / To fetch one if one goes astray, / To lift one if one totters down, / To strengthen whilst one stands.
entries.source: Christina Rossetti, Goblin Market, lines 562 to 567, Goblin Market and Other Poems (Macmillan, 1862) (Laura)
entries.note: Verified, the closing lines of the poem. Lifting one who totters is a trial line.

entries.quote: My heart is moved by all I cannot save: / so much has been destroyed / I have to cast my lot with those / who age after age, perversely, / with no extraordinary power, / reconstitute the world.
entries.source: Adrienne Rich, Natural Resources, closing six lines, The Dream of a Common Language (W. W. Norton, 1978)
entries.note: Verified against three postings crediting the 1978 edition; the Norton page itself was not opened. A trial line.

entries.quote: All letters, methinks, should be free and easy as one’s discourse; not studied as an oration, nor made up of hard words like a charm.
entries.source: Dorothy Osborne, Letters from Dorothy Osborne to Sir William Temple, Letter 33, pp. 160 to 161 (ed. Edward Abbott Parry, 1888)
entries.note: Corrected to Letter 33 in Parry’s edition of 1888, running across pages 160 and 161. The undated heading is kept as Parry prints it.

entries.quote: Freedom is always and exclusively freedom for the one who thinks differently.
entries.source: Rosa Luxemburg, The Russian Revolution, ch. 6, The Problem of Dictatorship (trans. Bertram D. Wolfe, 1940)
entries.note: Verified in Wolfe’s translation of 1940. Freedom for the one who thinks differently, a line about dissent.

entries.quote: Mrs. Dalloway said she would buy the flowers herself.
entries.source: Virginia Woolf, Mrs Dalloway, the opening sentence (1925)
entries.note: Verified opening line. Held: Mrs Dalloway buying the flowers herself is plain speech about a whole life, and it offers no counsel.

entries.quote: Listen to this reed how it complains: it is telling a tale of separations.
entries.source: Rumi, The Masnavi, Book I, line 1, the opening line (trans. Reynold A. Nicholson, 1926)

entries.quote: In spite of illness, in spite even of the arch-enemy sorrow, one can remain alive long past the usual date of disintegration if one is unafraid of change, insatiable in intellectual curiosity, interested in big things, and happy in small ways.
entries.source: Edith Wharton, A Backward Glance, A First Word, third paragraph (D. Appleton-Century, 1934)

entries.quote: Life is a pure flame, and we live by an invisible Sun within us.
entries.source: Thomas Browne, Hydriotaphia, Urn-Burial, chapter V (1658)

entries.quote: If by eternity is understood not endless temporal duration but timelessness, then he lives eternally who lives in the present.
entries.source: Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus, proposition 6.4311 (trans. C. K. Ogden, 1922)

entries.quote: Better by far you should forget and smile / Than that you should remember and be sad.
entries.source: Christina Rossetti, ‘Remember’, lines 13 to 14, Goblin Market and Other Poems (Macmillan, 1862)

entries.quote: Though leaves are many, the root is one; / Through all the lying days of my youth / I swayed my leaves and flowers in the sun; / Now I may wither into the truth.
entries.source: W. B. Yeats, The Coming of Wisdom with Time, the whole poem, The Green Helmet and Other Poems (Cuala Press, 1910)

entries.quote: We look at the world once, in childhood. / The rest is memory.
entries.source: Louise Glück, Nostos, the closing lines, Meadowlands (Ecco Press, 1996)

entries.quote: Eternity is in love with the productions of time.
entries.source: William Blake, The Marriage of Heaven and Hell, Proverbs of Hell, plate 7 (c. 1790 to 1793)
entries.note: Verified, the tenth Proverb of Hell, plate 7. Time and what is made in it: an impermanence line more than a discipline line.

entries.quote: Our life is March weather, savage and serene in one hour.
entries.source: Ralph Waldo Emerson, Representative Men, IV, Montaigne; or, the Skeptic (Phillips, Sampson and Company, 1850), p. 174
entries.note: Verified in the 1850 first edition, p. 174. It is about the inconstancy of moods, which is impermanence rather than renewal, and the March refuter named it the first to drop.

entries.quote: My candle burns at both ends; / It will not last the night; / But ah, my foes, and oh, my friends— / It gives a lovely light!
entries.source: Edna St. Vincent Millay, First Fig, the whole poem, A Few Figs from Thistles (Harper and Brothers, 1922)
entries.note: Corrected the edition to the Harper text of 1922. Held: a candle that will not last the night is impermanence.

entries.quote: The most exhausting thing in life, I have discovered, is being insincere.
entries.source: Anne Morrow Lindbergh, Gift from the Sea, chapter 2, Channelled Whelk (1955)
entries.note: Hedged: Gift from the Sea was never opened and the reference readings agree on chapter 2. Held for a month about sincerity.

entries.quote: Against the assault of laughter nothing can stand.
entries.source: Mark Twain, The Mysterious Stranger, ch. 10 (Satan) (Harper and Brothers, 1916)
entries.note: Verified. Held: laughter is the weapon here, not endurance, so it wants the lighter month.

entries.quote: But he that dares not grasp the thorn / Should never crave the rose.
entries.source: Anne Brontë, The Narrow Way (1848), lines 15 to 16, in The Complete Poems of Anne Brontë (ed. Clement Shorter, 1920), p. 145
entries.note: Verified in Shorter’s 1920 Complete Poems, p. 145: he that, not he who. Add the page to the source. Held to keep March under the cap for lines originally in English.

entries.quote: My way of joking is to tell the truth. It’s the funniest joke in the world.
entries.source: Bernard Shaw, John Bull’s Other Island, Act II, his reply to Nora Reilly (Peter Keegan)
entries.note: Verified as Peter Keegan’s reply to Nora Reilly. Held because the drama lane was already full.

entries.quote: I am large, I contain multitudes.
entries.source: Walt Whitman, Leaves of Grass, ‘Song of Myself’, section 51, 1881 text
entries.note: Verified; parenthetical in the source. Not a beginning line so much as a truth-and-clarity line.

entries.quote: The world of dew / Is the world of dew, / And yet . . . / And yet . . .
entries.source: Kobayashi Issa, The Year of My Life, pp. 103 to 104, the elegy for his daughter (trans. Nobuyuki Yuasa, 1960)
entries.note: Held, not refused: the verse ends on the translator’s ellipsis, so it cannot carry the terminal stop every card needs. It would need a translation that closes on a stop, and nothing else about it was in doubt.

entries.quote: To tame the Proud, the fetter’d Slave to free; / These are Imperial Arts, and worthy thee.
entries.source: Virgil, the Aeneid, Book VI, the close of Anchises’ speech, Latin 6.852 to 853 (Anchises) (trans. John Dryden, 1697, text of 1709)
entries.note: Corrected: the wording read is the 1709 Tonson octavo of Dryden, and the Latin is 6.852 to 853, not 6.853. The proposal line numbers 1177 and 1178 rest on a misplaced margin marker. Dryden’s fetter’d Slave to free renders parcere subiectis, spare the conquered; Anchises is naming the arts of empire.

entries.quote: Why is it always the innocents who suffer most, when you high lords play your game of thrones?
entries.source: George R. R. Martin, A Game of Thrones, chapter 58, Eddard XV (Bantam Books, 1996) (Varys, to Eddard Stark)
entries.note: The words are the tail of a longer sentence. Varys says If that’s true, Lord Eddard, tell me, before them, so the line is cut at the clause and its first letter raised. Calendar For Life credits A Clash of Kings; the chapter is Eddard XV in A Game of Thrones, where Varys visits Ned in the black cells.

entries.quote: Human beings have rights, because they are moral beings: the rights of all men grow out of their moral nature; and as all men have the same moral nature, they have essentially the same rights.
entries.source: Angelina Grimké, Letters to Catherine E. Beecher, Letter XII, Human Rights Not Founded on Sex, 2 October 1837 (Isaac Knapp, 1838)

entries.quote: Most that I have done and suffered in the service of our cause has been in public, and I have received much encouragement at every step of the way. You on the other hand have labored in a private way.
entries.source: Frederick Douglass, letter to Harriet Tubman, 29 August 1868, in Sarah H. Bradford, Scenes in the Life of Harriet Tubman, p. 7 (1869)
entries.note: Corrected the page. The letter begins at the foot of page 6 in the 1869 Auburn printing and these two sentences fall on page 7. Bradford’s book is named as the printing that carries the letter. The wording is exact, including on the other hand without commas.

entries.quote: As a woman, I have no country. As a woman I want no country. As a woman my country is the whole world.
entries.source: Virginia Woolf, Three Guineas, section Three, on ‘our’ country (Hogarth Press, 1938) (the outsider)
entries.note: Corrected the locator. The sentences stand in section Three, a page before the Society of Outsiders is named, so that heading was too far on. Woolf puts the words inside quotation marks in the mouth of the outsider, answering a demand that she fight for her country, and the cut raises her lower case as to a capital.

entries.quote: Justice is a habit whereby a man renders to each one his due by a constant and perpetual will.
entries.source: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologica, II-II, q. 58, a. 1, I answer that (trans. Fathers of the English Dominican Province, 1920)
entries.note: The line stands in the body of article 1, not in a reply to an objection. Aquinas offers it as a reformulation of the Roman jurists’ definition, introduced by if anyone would reduce it to the proper form of a definition, and he endorses it. The lifted clause takes a capital and a full stop.

entries.quote: My final prayer: O my body, make of me always a man who questions!
entries.source: Frantz Fanon, Black Skin, White Masks, Conclusion, the final sentence (trans. Charles Lam Markmann, 1967)

entries.quote: What is wanted for women is equal rights, equal admission to all social privileges; not a position apart, a sort of sentimental priesthood.
entries.source: Harriet Taylor Mill, Enfranchisement of Women, Westminster and Foreign Quarterly Review, July 1851, on the Worcester resolutions

entries.quote: Woman is born free and remains equal to man in rights.
entries.source: Olympe de Gouges, Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen, Article I (trans. Lynn Hunt, 1996)

entries.quote: We are the only animal species in which the female depends on the male for food, the only animal species in which the sex-relation is also an economic relation.
entries.source: Charlotte Perkins Gilman, Women and Economics, chapter I (Small, Maynard and Company, 1898)

entries.quote: I know you do not make the laws, but I also know that you are the wives and mothers, the sisters and daughters of those who do; and if you really suppose you can do nothing to overthrow slavery, you are greatly mistaken.
entries.source: Angelina Grimké, Appeal to the Christian Women of the South, answering why appeal to women, p. 16 (American Anti-Slavery Society, 1836)
entries.note: Corrected: in the 1836 pamphlet the sentence begins To this I reply, and the quotation starts at the clause that follows, every word in order. The page is added: the passage stands on page 16, answering the objection that women make no laws and have no legislative power.

entries.quote: I shall always be a flower girl to Professor Higgins, because he always treats me as a flower girl, and always will; but I know I can be a lady to you, because you always treat me as a lady, and always will.
entries.source: Bernard Shaw, Pygmalion, Act V, the speech to Colonel Pickering (Liza Doolittle)

entries.quote: Sometimes I think it ain’t right to stand and watch them do it.
entries.source: Lillian Hellman, The Little Foxes, Act Three, the close of the speech on those who eat the earth (Addie) (Viking Press, 1939)

entries.quote: Yes, I’d give the Devil benefit of law, for my own safety’s sake.
entries.source: Robert Bolt, A Man for All Seasons, Act One, the exchange with Roper (Heinemann, 1960) (Sir Thomas More)

entries.quote: Let a new earth rise. Let another world be born.
entries.source: Margaret Walker, For My People, the opening of the final stanza, Poetry, November 1937, and For My People (Yale, 1942)

entries.quote: Yes, injured Woman! rise, assert thy right!
entries.source: Anna Laetitia Barbauld, The Rights of Woman, line 1, Works, ed. Lucy Aikin, vol. I, p. 185 (Longman, 1825)
entries.note: Corrected the locator to page 185 of the 1825 Works, line 1. The poem was printed after Barbauld died and it turns against its own opening: the last stanza tells woman to abandon each ambitious thought and closes that separate rights are lost in mutual love.

entries.quote: Music to soothe all its sorrow, / Till war and crime shall cease; / And the hearts of men grown tender / Girdle the world with peace.
entries.source: Frances Ellen Watkins Harper, Songs for the People, the closing stanza, Poems (George S. Ferguson, 1896); first in Atlanta Offering, 1895

entries.quote: Surround yourself with human beings, my dear James. They are easier to fight for than principles.
entries.source: Ian Fleming, Casino Royale, chapter 20, The Nature of Evil (Jonathan Cape, 1953) (René Mathis)
entries.note: Verified in the chapter text; people over abstractions, spoken by Mathis. A service line.

entries.quote: I rebel—therefore we exist.
entries.source: Albert Camus, The Rebel, Part One, The Rebel (trans. Anthony Bower, 1953)
entries.note: Verified in Bower with his em dash, the last sentence of Part One; the real text behind Calendar For Life candidate 3. Camus stands at one for the year.

entries.quote: There is no religion without love, and people may talk as much as they like about their religion, but if it does not teach them to be good and kind to man and beast it is all a sham.
entries.source: Anna Sewell, Black Beauty, Part I, chapter 13 (John Manly)
entries.note: CORRECTED: Sewell’s sentence runs on, all a sham, James, and it won’t stand when things come to be turned inside out; the line is cut at the clause and given a full stop, and the first word is raised to a capital.

entries.quote: You become responsible, forever, for what you have tamed.
entries.source: Antoine de Saint-Exupéry, The Little Prince, chapter XXI (the fox) (trans. Katherine Woods, 1943)
entries.note: Verified in Woods, the fox’s own line. A responsibility line.

entries.quote: To will oneself free is also to will others free.
entries.source: Simone de Beauvoir, The Ethics of Ambiguity, Part II, Personal Freedom and Others (trans. Bernard Frechtman, 1948)
entries.note: Verified in Frechtman. Beauvoir stands at one for the year.

entries.quote: How selfish soever man may be supposed, there are evidently some principles in his nature, which interest him in the fortune of others, and render their happiness necessary to him, though he derives nothing from it except the pleasure of seeing it.
entries.source: Adam Smith, The Theory of Moral Sentiments, Part I, Section I, Chapter I, Of Sympathy (6th edition, 1790)
entries.note: Verified: the opening sentence of the book in the 6th edition.

entries.quote: Yet minds are not conquered by force, but by love and high-mindedness.
entries.source: Baruch Spinoza, Ethics, Part IV, Appendix, XI (trans. R. H. M. Elwes, 1883)
entries.note: Verified in Elwes. January routed Spinoza’s closing sentence to March; one Spinoza per month.

entries.quote: Here is thy footstool and there rest thy feet where live the poorest, and lowliest, and lost.
entries.source: Rabindranath Tagore, Gitanjali (Song Offerings), poem 10, opening sentence (the author’s own English, 1912)
entries.note: Verified in the Macmillan text; a prose poem, so no line breaks. January routed Light, my light to December; one Tagore per month.

entries.quote: Yet such is oft the course of deeds that move the wheels of the world: small hands do them because they must, while the eyes of the great are elsewhere.
entries.source: J. R. R. Tolkien, The Fellowship of the Ring, Book II, chapter 2, The Council of Elrond (Elrond) (George Allen and Unwin, 1954), p. 283
entries.note: Verified on p. 283 of the 1954 Allen and Unwin text by search-inside; the opening word Yet was outside the snippet and rests on secondary witnesses. Add p. 283 to the source. A service line. Mind the Tolkien count: the carry holds several.

entries.quote: The pitcher cries for water to carry / and a person for work that is real.
entries.source: Marge Piercy, To be of use, Circles on the Water (1982), closing lines; first in To Be of Use (1973)
entries.note: Verified against the Poetry Foundation text, credited to Circles on the Water (1982); nobody has seen the 1973 page. Honest source: Marge Piercy, To be of use, Circles on the Water (1982), closing lines; first in To Be of Use (1973). To be of use is September’s theme.

entries.quote: Travel is fatal to prejudice, bigotry and narrow-mindedness, and many of our people need it sorely on these accounts.
entries.source: Mark Twain, The Innocents Abroad, the Conclusion (American Publishing Company, 1869)
entries.note: Verified travel line held: it widens the circle rather than counselling, and Twain is unused in the year.

entries.quote: The founding of libraries was like constructing more public granaries, amassing reserves against a spiritual winter.
entries.source: Marguerite Yourcenar, Memoirs of Hadrian, Tellus Stabilita (Hadrian) (trans. Grace Frick, 1954)
entries.note: Corrected: the full stop marks a cut at a complete clause. Held: libraries as granaries is a public duty, not private counsel.

entries.quote: I do not care what case you put; let them be sea-captains, if you will.
entries.source: Margaret Fuller, Woman in the Nineteenth Century, on the offices women may fill (ed. Arthur B. Fuller, 1855)
entries.note: Verified. Held: let them be sea-captains is an argument about what is owed to women.

entries.quote: If all Men are born Free, how is it that all Women are born Slaves?
entries.source: Mary Astell, Some Reflections upon Marriage, the 1706 Preface, printed as the Appendix in the fourth edition, 1730, p. 150
entries.note: Verified. Held: Astell’s question is a demand for justice, not counsel.

entries.quote: We live close together and we live far apart. We all go through the same things—it’s all just a different kind of the same thing.
entries.source: Susan Glaspell, Trifles, the one act, near the close (Mrs. Hale) (Plays, Small, Maynard and Company, 1920)
entries.note: Verified. Held: Mrs Hale on going through the same things is about the debt between neighbours.

entries.quote: The good life is one inspired by love and guided by knowledge.
entries.source: Bertrand Russell, What I Believe, chapter II, The Good Life (E. P. Dutton, 1925), p. 20
entries.note: Verified in the Dutton text of 1925. Held: the good life inspired by love and guided by knowledge is a public creed.

entries.quote: I am in fact a Hobbit (in all but size).
entries.source: J. R. R. Tolkien, The Letters of J. R. R. Tolkien, letter 213, to Deborah Webster, 25 October 1958 (ed. Humphrey Carpenter, 1981)
entries.note: Verified in letter 213 of the Carpenter edition. A self knowledge line with a homely turn.

entries.quote: The door itself / makes no promises. / It is only a door.
entries.source: Adrienne Rich, Prospective Immigrants Please Note, closing lines, Snapshots of a Daughter-in-Law (Harper and Row, 1963)
entries.note: Corrected publisher: Harper and Row published the book in 1963 and Norton reissued it in 1967.

entries.quote: I can’t do much with my hands; so I will make a battering-ram of my head and make a way through this rough-and-tumble world.
entries.source: Louisa May Alcott, Her Life, Letters, and Journals, letter to her father of 29 November 1856, p. 89 (ed. Ednah D. Cheney, 1889)
entries.note: Corrected: this is not a journal entry of 1850. Cheney prints it in chapter five, Authorship, inside a letter written from Boston to her father on 29 November 1856, her twenty-fourth birthday, on page 89 of the Roberts Brothers edition. The tag becomes Correspondence. The wording is exact.

entries.quote: I will not be ‘famous’, ‘great’. I will go on adventuring, changing, opening my mind and my eyes, refusing to be stamped and stereotyped.
entries.source: Virginia Woolf, A Writer’s Diary, the entry of 29 October 1933 (ed. Leonard Woolf, Hogarth Press, 1953)
entries.note: Verified. Held for a later month.

entries.quote: But I ask no favors for my sex. I surrender not our claim to equality. All I ask of our brethren is, that they will take their feet from off our necks, and permit us to stand upright on that ground which God designed us to occupy.
entries.source: Sarah Moore Grimké, Letters on the Equality of the Sexes, Letter II, Woman Subject Only to God, p. 10 (Isaac Knapp, 1838)
entries.note: Verified. Held: the Correspondence lane took three and this one belongs with Fuller and Cooper.

entries.quote: We never know how high we are / Till we are called to rise; / And then, if we are true to plan, / Our statures touch the skies.
entries.source: Emily Dickinson, ‘We never know how high we are’ (Fr1197, J1176), Poems, Third Series, ed. Mabel Loomis Todd, Life XIV (1896)
entries.note: Corrected: Aspiration is Todd title, not Dickinson, so the poem is cited by first line and standard numbers. Held: Dickinson stands at two for the year and the last slot should be chosen deliberately.

entries.quote: Trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string.
entries.source: Ralph Waldo Emerson, Essays: First Series, Self-Reliance (James Munroe, 1841)
entries.note: Verified. Held: Trust thyself is self-reliance under pressure more than counsel from an elder.

entries.quote: As firmly cemented clam shells / Fall apart in autumn, / So I must take to the road again, / Farewell, my friends.
entries.source: Matsuo Bashō, The Narrow Road to the Deep North, the closing verse at Ogaki (trans. Nobuyuki Yuasa, 1966)

entries.quote: I had a farm in Africa, at the foot of the Ngong Hills.
entries.source: Isak Dinesen, Out of Africa, Book One, The Ngong Farm, the opening sentence (Putnam, 1937)

entries.quote: For nothing is fixed, forever and forever and forever, it is not fixed; the earth is always shifting, the light is always changing, the sea does not cease to grind down rock.
entries.source: James Baldwin, Nothing Personal, the closing passage (Atheneum, 1964)

entries.quote: Though a country be sundered, hills and rivers endure; / And spring comes green again to trees and grasses / Where petals have been shed like tears / And lonely birds have sung their grief.
entries.source: Du Fu, A Spring View, lines 1 to 4, The Jade Mountain, p. 148 (trans. Witter Bynner with Kiang Kang-hu, 1929)

entries.quote: But not because of its magnificence / Dear is the Casuarina to my soul: / Beneath it we have played; though years may roll, / O sweet companions, loved with love intense, / For your sakes, shall the tree be ever dear.
entries.source: Toru Dutt, Our Casuarina Tree, stanza 3, lines 1 to 5, Ancient Ballads and Legends of Hindustan (Kegan Paul, Trench and Co., 1882)
entries.note: Corrected the locator. Each stanza of the poem runs to eleven lines and the quotation is only the first five of stanza three, so the locator now names those lines. The wording stands as printed, with the colon after soul and the comma after sakes.

entries.quote: Barrabás came to us by sea, the child Clara wrote in her delicate calligraphy.
entries.source: Isabel Allende, The House of the Spirits, chapter 1, the opening sentence (trans. Magda Bogin, 1985)
entries.note: Verified opening line in Bogin’s translation; it returns as the novel’s last line. Held for a month that can use a pure opening.

entries.quote: The butterfly counts not months but moments, / and has time enough.
entries.source: Rabindranath Tagore, Fireflies, p. 15 (Macmillan, New York, 1928)
entries.note: Corrected in re-verification to a page locator. Held: a two line poem about moments, for the month of passing things.

entries.quote: He could see plainly that she was not herself. That is, he could not see that she was becoming herself and daily casting aside that fictitious self which we assume like a garment with which to appear before the world.
entries.source: Kate Chopin, The Awakening, chapter XIX (1899)
entries.note: Verified in chapter XIX of 1899. Casting aside the fictitious self, which is a truth line held for want of a day.

entries.quote: Some men say an army of horse and some men say an army on foot and some men say an army of ships is the most beautiful thing on the black earth. But I say it is what you love.
entries.source: Sappho, If Not, Winter, Fragment 16, lines 1 to 4 (trans. Anne Carson, 2002)
entries.note: Carried from January, verified in Carson, p. 27. Before it lands, the four lines must be marked with slashes in Carson’s lineation, which nobody has yet checked against the page; it is carried as prose.

entries.quote: I will mount a long wind some day and break the heavy waves / And set my cloudy sail straight and bridge the deep, deep sea.
entries.source: Li Bai, The Hard Road, closing couplet, The Jade Mountain, p. 70 (trans. Witter Bynner, 1929)
entries.note: Verified. One Bynner poem landed already and only one may stand in a month, and the hard road is a courage line.

entries.quote: The wide world is all about you: you can fence yourselves in, but you cannot for ever fence it out.
entries.source: J. R. R. Tolkien, The Fellowship of the Ring, Book I, chapter 3, Three is Company (George Allen and Unwin, 1954) (Gildor Inglorion)
entries.note: Verified with the two-word for ever. Tolkien’s small hands is already held for September, so this goes to July.

entries.quote: A very strange and solemn feeling came over me as I stood there, with no sound but the rustle of the pines, no one near me, and the sun so glorious, as for me alone.
entries.source: Louisa May Alcott, Her Life, Letters, and Journals, ch. III, Fruitlands, journal entry headed Concord, Thursday (ed. Cheney, 1889)

entries.quote: In the highlands you woke up in the morning and thought: Here I am, where I ought to be.
entries.source: Isak Dinesen, Out of Africa, Book One, Kamante and Lulu, ch. 1, The Ngong Farm (Putnam, 1937)
entries.note: Corrected the locator. Book One is titled Kamante and Lulu and The Ngong Farm is its first chapter, so the proposal gave the chapter title in the place of the book title. The wording is exact. Blixen wrote the book in English, so no translator is named.

entries.quote: Every one knows what attention is. It is the taking possession by the mind, in clear and vivid form, of one out of what seem several simultaneously possible objects or trains of thought.
entries.source: William James, The Principles of Psychology, vol. I, ch. XI, ‘Attention’, pp. 403 to 404 (Henry Holt, 1890)

entries.quote: For all the toll the desert takes of a man it gives compensations, deep breaths, deep sleep, and the communion of the stars.
entries.source: Mary Austin, The Land of Little Rain, ch. 1, ‘The Land of Little Rain’ (Houghton Mifflin, 1903)

entries.quote: Mysticism is the art of union with Reality.
entries.source: Evelyn Underhill, Practical Mysticism, ch. I, ‘What is Mysticism?’, the displayed definition (1914)

entries.quote: This being the case, if I were asked to name the chief benefit of the house, I should say: the house shelters daydreaming, the house protects the dreamer, the house allows one to dream in peace.
entries.source: Gaston Bachelard, The Poetics of Space, ch. 1, ‘The House. From Cellar to Garret’, p. 6 (trans. Maria Jolas, 1964)
entries.note: Corrected the wording against the Jolas scan at the Internet Archive. The sentence begins This being the case, and the edition spells daydreaming as one word: the hyphen that circulates online is an end of line break in the scan. The page, 6, is added.

entries.quote: Silence remains, inescapably, a form of speech (in many instances, of complaint or indictment) and an element in a dialogue.
entries.source: Susan Sontag, Styles of Radical Will, ‘The Aesthetics of Silence’, the opening essay (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1969)

entries.quote: Thou hast come to a steed-famed land for rest, / O stranger worn with toil, / To a land of all lands the goodliest / Colonus’ glistening soil.
entries.source: Sophocles, Oedipus at Colonus, the Colonus ode, first strophe, from line 668 (the Chorus) (trans. F. Storr, 1912)

entries.quote: Thousands at his bidding speed / And post o’re Land and Ocean without rest: / They also serve who only stand and waite.
entries.source: John Milton, When I consider how my light is spent, lines 12 to 14, Poems (1673)
entries.note: Corrected the edition. The old spellings o’re and waite belong to the Poems of 1673, verified in the Milton Reading Room text of that edition. Beeching’s Oxford text of 1900 was not opened and is not claimed. The quotation begins inside line 12, which opens Is Kingly.

entries.quote: Up the dome of heaven / Like a great hill, / I watch them marching / Stately and still, / And I know that I / Am honored to be / Witness / Of so much majesty.
entries.source: Sara Teasdale, Stars, the last two stanzas, lines 13 to 20, Flame and Shadow, Part I (Macmillan, 1920)
entries.note: Corrected: the poem runs to twenty lines in five stanzas, so its closing two stanzas are lines 13 to 20 and not lines 17 to 24. The wording, capitals and punctuation are those of the 1920 text. The alternating indents of the printed page cannot be shown in a single line.

entries.quote: Let it come, as it will, and don’t / be afraid. God does not leave us / comfortless, so let evening come.
entries.source: Jane Kenyon, Let Evening Come, the final stanza, lines 16 to 18 (Graywolf Press, 1990)

entries.quote: We call it a grain of sand, / but it calls itself neither grain nor sand.
entries.source: Wisława Szymborska, View with a Grain of Sand, lines 1 to 2, Ludzie na moście (1986) (trans. Stanisław Barańczak and Clare Cavanagh, 1995)

entries.quote: Listen to the reed how it tells a tale, complaining of separations.
entries.source: Rumi, Masnavi, Book I, line 1 (trans. Reynold A. Nicholson, 1926)
entries.note: Verified opening line. Nicholson later revised it after the oldest manuscript to Listen to this reed how it complains; the 1926 wording ships with the 1926 date. Held for a quieter month.

entries.quote: In a hole in the ground there lived a hobbit.
entries.source: J. R. R. Tolkien, The Hobbit, ch. 1, ‘An Unexpected Party’, first sentence
entries.note: Verified opening line, pure delight; January had more openings than days. Mind the cap: the Calendar For Life bank carries many Tolkien lines.

entries.quote: I’ve learned to live simply, wisely, / To look at the sky and pray to God, / And to take long walks before evening / To wear out this useless anxiety.
entries.source: Anna Akhmatova, ‘I’ve learned to live simply, wisely’ (1912), Rosary (1914), lines 1 to 4 (trans. Judith Hemschemeyer, 1990)
entries.note: Verified on several independent reprints credited to Hemschemeyer, confidence medium: the Zephyr volume was not opened and no page is cited. Tidier source: Rosary (1914). A quiet daily practice: October.

entries.quote: Patience, patience, patience, is what the sea teaches. Patience and faith. One should lie empty, open, choiceless as a beach—waiting for a gift from the sea.
entries.source: Anne Morrow Lindbergh, Gift from the Sea, chapter 1, The Beach (Pantheon, 1955)
entries.note: Verified. It is a stillness line, not a road line.

entries.quote: When the spirit swells my breast I love to roam leisurely among the green hills; or sometimes, sitting on the brink of the murmuring Missouri, I marvel at the great blue overhead.
entries.source: Zitkala-Ša, The Great Spirit, American Indian Stories, opening sentence (Hayworth Publishing House, 1921)
entries.note: Verified. The refuter called its fit for April honest rather than exact: it is a marvelling line, so it goes to the month of stillness.

entries.quote: The time that my journey takes is long and the way of it long. I came out on the chariot of the first gleam of light, and pursued my voyage through the wildernesses of worlds leaving my track on many a star and planet.
entries.source: Rabindranath Tagore, Gitanjali (Song Offerings), poem 12, opening two paragraphs (trans. the author, 1912)
entries.note: Verified. The long journey inward, which suits the month of stillness better than the month of setting out.

entries.quote: One day as I was sitting alone in my study surrounded by books on all kinds of subjects, devoting myself to literary studies, my usual habit, my mind dwelt at length on the weighty opinions of various authors whom I had studied for a long time.
entries.source: Christine de Pizan, The Book of the City of Ladies, Part One, ch. 1, the opening sentence (trans. Earl Jeffrey Richards, 1982)
entries.note: Corrected: the whole opening sentence is restored from the Richards translation. Held: it sets a scene in a study, which suits the month of the quiet room.

entries.quote: Do nothing which is of no use.
entries.source: Miyamoto Musashi, A Book of Five Rings, the Ground Book, the last of the nine rules for learning the Way (trans. Victor Harris, 1974)
entries.note: Verified, medium confidence on the Harris translation. Held: do nothing which is of no use is a rule of attention.

entries.quote: Men may dyen of ymaginacioun, / So depe may impressioun be take.
entries.source: Geoffrey Chaucer, The Canterbury Tales, The Miller’s Tale, lines 3612 to 3613, The Riverside Chaucer (the Miller)
entries.note: Verified in the Riverside lineation. Middle English on the page, which suits a month with room for older spelling.

entries.quote: I hope it is no very cynical asperity not to confess obligations where no benefit has been received, or to be unwilling that the Publick should consider me as owing that to a Patron, which Providence has enabled me to do for myself.
entries.source: Samuel Johnson, letter to Lord Chesterfield, 7 February 1755, in Boswell, Life of Johnson, under 1755
entries.note: Corrected to the wording Boswell prints, with obligations in the plural and Publick in the old spelling. The manuscript behind the Hyde edition differs again.

entries.quote: I’ll make my report as if I told a story, for I was taught as a child on my homeworld that Truth is a matter of the imagination.
entries.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, The Left Hand of Darkness, chapter 1, opening sentence (Genly Ai)
entries.note: Verified as the first sentence of Genly Ai’s report. Truth as a matter of the imagination, which is a strong line for any month about story.

entries.quote: The writer should never be ashamed of staring. There is nothing that doesn’t require his attention.
entries.source: Flannery O’Connor, Mystery and Manners, The Nature and Aim of Fiction (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1969)
entries.note: Verified in Mystery and Manners. Attention as a discipline, which suits a month about looking.

entries.quote: I, too, dislike it.
entries.source: Marianne Moore, Poetry, line 1, Complete Poems (Macmillan and Viking, 1967)
entries.note: Corrected to the three line final text of 1967, because the printings of 1919 and 1924 read I too, dislike it with one comma.

entries.quote: The universe is made of stories, / not of atoms.
entries.source: Muriel Rukeyser, The Speed of Darkness, section IX (Random House, 1968)
entries.note: Verified in section IX of The Speed of Darkness. Stories rather than atoms, a line about what the world is made of.

entries.quote: We tell ourselves stories in order to live.
entries.source: Joan Didion, The White Album, the title essay, opening sentence (Simon and Schuster, 1979)
entries.note: Verified opening line. The essay goes on to test the claim, so the line is cooler than it reads alone; a truth-and-clarity line.

entries.quote: Man is least himself when he talks in his own person. Give him a mask, and he will tell you the truth.
entries.source: Oscar Wilde, The Critic as Artist, Part II, in Intentions, 1891 (Gilbert)
entries.note: Verified. Held: the mask line is about how truth gets said, so it wants the month of plain speech.

entries.quote: Do you not see how necessary a World of Pains and troubles is to school an Intelligence and make it a soul?
entries.source: John Keats, letter to George and Georgiana Keats, 14 February to 3 May 1819, the entry of 21 April (ed. Gittings, 1970)
entries.note: Verified. Held: the world of pains that schools an intelligence is a line about becoming, not about holding.

entries.quote: The unknown, the unforetold, the unproven, that is what life is based on. Ignorance is the ground of thought. Unproof is the ground of action.
entries.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, The Left Hand of Darkness, ch. 5, The Domestication of Hunch (Faxe) (1969)
entries.note: Corrected: the novel reads the unproven, not the unprovable. Held: ignorance as the ground of thought is a line about not knowing rather than about courage.

entries.quote: Nevertheless, not to extinguish our free will, I hold it to be true that Fortune is the arbiter of one-half of our actions, but that she still leaves us to direct the other half, or perhaps a little less.
entries.source: Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince, chapter XXV (trans. W. K. Marriott, 1908)
entries.note: Verified. Held: fortune and the half we still direct is a line about agency, and the Philosophy lane was full.

entries.quote: To conquer fear is the beginning of wisdom, in the pursuit of truth as in the endeavour after a worthy manner of life.
entries.source: Bertrand Russell, Unpopular Essays, ch. 7, An Outline of Intellectual Rubbish (George Allen and Unwin, 1950)
entries.note: Corrected: the spelling follows the George Allen and Unwin text, which reads endeavour. Held: to conquer fear is the beginning of wisdom sits close to Kant, and Kant took the day.

entries.quote: What is there / like fortitude! What sap / went through that little thread / to make the cherry red!
entries.source: Marianne Moore, Nevertheless, the last four lines, in the collection Nevertheless (Macmillan, 1944)
entries.note: Corrected: the quotation now starts at What is there, so the verse keeps Moore own line breaks. Held: the Poetry lane was the fattest in the month.

entries.quote: Tell me about a complicated man.
entries.source: Homer, The Odyssey, Book 1, line 1 (trans. Emily Wilson, 2017)
entries.note: Verified opening line of Wilson’s Odyssey. Held because January had more openings than days; a line for hard roads.

entries.quote: Yes, of course it hurts when buds are breaking. Why else would the springtime falter?
entries.source: Karin Boye, Yes, Of Course It Hurts, lines 1 and 2, För trädets skull (1935) (trans. David McDuff, 1994)
entries.note: Verified in McDuff. Held because April landed the other Boye, and one person may stand once a month; the pain of growth suits the month of courage.

entries.quote: Living is no laughing matter: / you must live with great seriousness / like a squirrel, for example— / I mean without looking for something beyond and above living, / I mean living must be your whole occupation.
entries.source: Nâzim Hikmet, On Living, Part I, opening lines, in Poems of Nazim Hikmet (trans. Randy Blasing and Mutlu Konuk, 1994)
entries.note: Verified. Held: living with great seriousness is a charge to hold on, which is July.

entries.quote: I wished to tell the truth, for truth always conveys its own moral to those who are able to receive it.
entries.source: Anne Brontë, The Tenant of Wildfell Hall, Preface to the Second Edition, 22 July 1848
entries.note: Verified in the Preface to the second edition of 1848. A plain statement of purpose.

entries.quote: You can’t get away from yourself by moving from one place to another.
entries.source: Ernest Hemingway, The Sun Also Rises, Book I, chapter 2 (Jake Barnes)
entries.note: Verified, Jake to Robert Cohn. It corrects the traveller rather than sending him out, so it reads as a truth line and not an April line.

entries.quote: Some races wax and others wane, and in a short space the tribes of living things are changed, and like runners hand on the torch of life.
entries.source: Lucretius, De Rerum Natura, Book II, lines 77 to 79 (trans. Cyril Bailey, 1910)

entries.quote: Duration is the continuous progress of the past which gnaws into the future and which swells as it advances.
entries.source: Henri Bergson, Creative Evolution, chapter I (trans. Arthur Mitchell, 1911)

entries.quote: Life is not a series of gig lamps symmetrically arranged; life is a luminous halo, a semi-transparent envelope surrounding us from the beginning of consciousness to the end.
entries.source: Virginia Woolf, Modern Fiction, The Common Reader (Hogarth Press, 1925)
entries.note: Corrected the wording. The Common Reader of 1925 reads life is a luminous halo. The reading but a luminous halo belongs to the earlier version of the essay, Modern Novels, printed in the Times Literary Supplement in 1919.

entries.quote: I think we are well advised to keep on nodding terms with the people we used to be, whether we find them attractive company or not.
entries.source: Joan Didion, Slouching Towards Bethlehem, On Keeping a Notebook (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1968)

entries.quote: The public must decide whether it wishes to continue on the present road, and it can do so only when in full possession of the facts.
entries.source: Rachel Carson, Silent Spring, chapter 2, The Obligation to Endure (Houghton Mifflin, 1962)
entries.note: Verified in chapter 2 of Silent Spring. Full possession of the facts, a public truth line.

entries.quote: I’m nobody! Who are you? / Are you nobody, too?
entries.source: Emily Dickinson, ‘I’m nobody! Who are you?’, Poems, Second Series, Life I, lines 1 to 2 (Roberts Brothers, 1891)
entries.note: Verified in Poems, Second Series of 1891. Two lines only, in that edition’s lineation.

entries.quote: Beauty is no quality in things themselves: It exists merely in the mind which contemplates them; and each mind perceives a different beauty.
entries.source: David Hume, Essays, Moral, Political, and Literary, Of the Standard of Taste (ed. Miller, pp. 229 to 230)
entries.note: Corrected in re-verification. Held: Hume sets the sentence out as the sceptical case and the next paragraph restrains it, so it wants a month about seeing clearly.

entries.quote: Music was my refuge. I could crawl into the spaces between the notes and curl my back to loneliness.
entries.source: Maya Angelou, Singin’ and Swingin’ and Gettin’ Merry Like Christmas, chapter 1, the opening sentences (Random House, 1976)
entries.note: Verified. Held: Maya Angelou stands in July with Still I Rise, and one person may stand once a month.

entries.quote: That’s no way to treat adventures. Never say ‘no’ to adventures. Always say ‘yes’, otherwise you’ll lead a very dull life.
entries.source: Ian Fleming, Chitty-Chitty-Bang-Bang: The Magical Car, Adventure Number Two (Commander Caractacus Pott) (Jonathan Cape, 1964)
entries.note: Verified. Held: Commander Pott’s counsel is about saying yes to danger, which suits a month of trial.

entries.quote: In Louisville, at the corner of Fourth and Walnut, in the center of the shopping district, I was suddenly overwhelmed with the realization that I loved all those people, that they were mine and I theirs, that we could not be alien to one another even though we were total strangers.
entries.source: Thomas Merton, Conjectures of a Guilty Bystander, Part Three, The Night Spirit and the Dawn Air (Doubleday, 1966)
entries.note: Corrected the tradition from Diary to Essay. Conjectures prints no dated entries. It is arranged in five titled parts, and the book describes itself as notes, opinions, experiences and reflections based on notebooks Merton kept since 1956. Part Three appeared as an essay in New Blackfriars in 1965. Merton’s dated journal is the separate A Search for Solitude.

entries.quote: Caring involves stepping out of one’s own personal frame of reference into the other’s.
entries.source: Nel Noddings, Caring: A Feminine Approach to Ethics and Moral Education, ch. 1, p. 24 (University of California Press, 1984)

entries.quote: Your silence will not protect you.
entries.source: Audre Lorde, Sister Outsider, The Transformation of Silence into Language and Action, p. 41 (The Crossing Press, 1984)
entries.note: Corrected: this is not new prose of 1984. Lorde delivered it as a paper at the Modern Language Association panel on lesbians and literature on 28 December 1977, and it was first printed in Sinister Wisdom in 1978. The wording and page given are those of Sister Outsider.

entries.quote: To sin by silence, when we should protest, / Makes cowards out of men. The human race / Has climbed on protest.
entries.source: Ella Wheeler Wilcox, Protest, lines 1 to 3, Poems of Problems, p. 154 (W. B. Conkey, 1914)

entries.quote: Good prose is like a window pane.
entries.source: George Orwell, Why I Write, the final paragraph (Gangrel, No. 4, Summer 1946)
entries.note: Verified in the final paragraph of Gangrel, Summer 1946. Held because Orwell can stand once in a month.

entries.quote: God offers to every mind its choice between truth and repose.
entries.source: Ralph Waldo Emerson, Intellect, essay XI in Essays: First Series (1841)
entries.note: Verified in essay XI of Essays: First Series. Truth or repose, and the choice is the whole line.

entries.quote: He that would seriously set upon the search of truth, ought in the first place to prepare his mind with a love of it.
entries.source: John Locke, An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Book IV, ch. XIX, Of Enthusiasm, section 1 (ed. Fraser, 1894, vol. II, p. 428)
entries.note: Corrected against Fraser’s Clarendon edition of 1894, which keeps the comma after truth. Of Enthusiasm was added in the fourth edition of 1700.

entries.quote: Never did eye see the sun unless it had first become sunlike, and never can the soul have vision of the First Beauty unless itself be beautiful.
entries.source: Plotinus, Enneads, I.6.9, On Beauty (trans. Stephen MacKenna, 1917)
entries.note: Verified in MacKenna 1917. A clarity line rather than a beginning line.

entries.quote: For to be possessed of a vigorous mind is not enough; the prime requisite is rightly to apply it.
entries.source: René Descartes, Discourse on the Method, Part I, first paragraph (trans. John Veitch, 1850)
entries.note: Verified in Veitch; the 1850 date is from memory, not from a scan. Right application of the mind: a clarity line.

entries.quote: The limits of my language mean the limits of my world.
entries.source: Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus, proposition 5.6 (trans. C. K. Ogden, 1922)
entries.note: Verified. Held because Wittgenstein can appear once in a month and proposition 7 is the stronger line for a quieter month.

entries.quote: Reading maketh a full man; conference a ready man; and writing an exact man.
entries.source: Francis Bacon, Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral, Of Studies (1625)
entries.note: Verified. Held only because Bacon lands in May with Read not to contradict; one person a month.

entries.quote: All men by nature desire to know.
entries.source: Aristotle, Metaphysics, Book I, ch. 1, 980a21 (trans. W. D. Ross, 1908)
entries.note: Verified opening of the Metaphysics. Held: all men by nature desire to know is the appetite for truth.

entries.quote: The answer must be, I think, that beauty and grace are performed whether or not we will or sense them. The least we can do is try to be there.
entries.source: Annie Dillard, Pilgrim at Tinker Creek, chapter 1, Heaven and Earth in Jest (Harper’s Magazine Press, 1974)

entries.quote: I did not care what it was all about. All I wanted to know was how to live in it. Maybe if you found out how to live in it you learned from that what it was all about.
entries.source: Ernest Hemingway, The Sun Also Rises, Book II, chapter 14 (Jake Barnes) (Charles Scribner’s Sons, 1926)
entries.note: Verified in the Scribner text of 1926. Held: Jake wants to know how to live in it, which is a search for clarity.

entries.quote: There is no foreign land; it is the traveller only that is foreign, and now and again, by a flash of recollection, lights up the contrasts of the earth.
entries.source: Robert Louis Stevenson, The Silverado Squatters, Part II, With the Children of Israel, chapter III, The Return (Chatto and Windus, 1883)
entries.note: Corrected: the sentence is in The Return, Part II. Held: it is the traveller only that is foreign is a correction of the eye, which is June.

retired.quote: If a man should importune me to give a reason why I loved him, I find it could no otherwise be expressed, than by making answer: because it was he, because it was I.
retired.source: Michel de Montaigne, Essays, Book I, chapter 27, Of Friendship (trans. Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt, 1877)
retired.note: Verified in Cotton and Hazlitt, whose numbering is 27 (28 in Villey). January routed Montaigne’s good faith to June; one Montaigne per month.

retired.why: hannah arendt reached the cap of three for the year
retired.quote: Forgiving, in other words, is the only reaction which does not merely re-act but acts anew and unexpectedly, unconditioned by the act which provoked it and therefore freeing from its consequences both the one who forgives and the one who is forgiven.
retired.source: Hannah Arendt, The Human Condition, chapter V, section 33, Irreversibility and the Power to Forgive (Chicago, 1958), p. 241
retired.note: Verified against the Chicago text. Arendt stands at one for the year; forgiveness as beginning anew is a December line.

retired.quote: Wherefore my counsel is, that we hold fast ever to the heavenly way and follow after justice and virtue always, considering that the soul is immortal and able to endure every sort of good and every sort of evil. Thus shall we live dear to one another and to the gods, both while remaining here and when, like conquerors in the games who go round to gather gifts, we receive our reward. And it shall be well with us both in this life and in the pilgrimage of a thousand years which we have been describing.
retired.source: Plato, The Republic, Book X, 621c to d, the closing lines (Socrates) (trans. Benjamin Jowett, 1888)
retired.note: CORRECTED: the translator year is 1888, Jowett's third edition, which is the setting whose page was read. The closing lines of the Republic, and about the soul that outlasts the road.

retired.quote: Conceptually, we may call truth what we cannot change; metaphorically, it is the ground on which we stand and the sky that stretches above us.
retired.source: Hannah Arendt, Truth and Politics, in Between Past and Future, closing sentence, p. 264 (Viking, 1968)
retired.note: Verified as the closing sentence of Truth and Politics. Held because the month was already full of ground and sky.

retired.quote: Do any human beings ever realize life while they live it?
retired.source: Thornton Wilder, Our Town, Act III, the graveyard scene (Emily)
retired.note: Corrected to the graveyard scene and to Emily, since in Act III she is married. No edition was opened, so the reading rests on eight published books.

retired.quote: The greatest benefit we owe to the artist, whether painter, poet, or novelist, is the extension of our sympathies.
retired.source: George Eliot, The Natural History of German Life, Westminster Review, July 1856; in Essays of George Eliot, ed. Sheppard (1883), essay V
retired.note: Verified twice in the Sheppard edition; refuted only as a month collision with the Middlemarch line, which landed. Eliot stands at two for the year after February.

retired.source: Blaise Pascal, Pensées, Brunschvicg fragment 347 (trans. W. F. Trotter, 1910)
retired.note: Corrected punctuation. The Trotter translation of 1910, printed in the Harvard Classics volume of Pascal, sets a comma after in nature where the proposal set a semicolon. Two separate scans of that printing agree. The semicolon belongs to the later Everyman printing of the same translation, so the year and the wording must match.

retired.note: The cosmology at 37d is spoken by Timaeus of Locri, not by Plato in his own voice, so the speaker is named after the locator, as the year’s other Plato lines do. The Jowett wording is unchanged and was checked against the 1892 text.

retired.source: Simone Weil, Gravity and Grace, Detachment, p. 59 (trans. Arthur Wills, 1952)
retired.note: Corrected the locator. The sentence stands in the chapter Detachment on page 59 of the Wills translation, published by Putnam in New York in 1952, not on page 13. The wording is verbatim in that text.

retired.source: Miguel de Cervantes, Don Quixote, Part II, chapter 42 (Don Quixote, to Sancho Panza) (trans. John Ormsby, 1885)
retired.note: Verified in Ormsby. Compassion tempered by justice: a September line.

retired.source: Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, ch. 4, answering Rousseau
retired.note: Verified in the 1792 text, immediately after the Rousseau quotation. Carried to March and not used, to hold the count of lines originally in English; power over themselves is also what September means by justice.

retired.quote: It is not enough to be industrious; so are the ants. What are you industrious about?
retired.source: Henry David Thoreau, Familiar Letters, ed. F. B. Sanborn, to Harrison Blake, Concord, 16 November 1857, p. 371 (Houghton Mifflin, 1894)
retired.note: Verified letter to Harrison Blake. Held: Thoreau asks what the industry is for, which is a question about service.

retired.note: Corrected: the proposal cut the sentence short and closed it with a full stop no edition prints. The 1847 Smith, Elder first edition, volume II, chapter VIII, runs on to which I now exert to leave you, with a semicolon before it. Held: Charlotte Bronte stands in July with Life.

retired.quote: Attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity.
retired.source: Simone Weil, letter to Joë Bousquet, 13 April 1942 (trans. Raymond Rosenthal, 1976, in Pétrement, Simone Weil: A Life, p. 462)
retired.note: Carried from January and held again: February took Weil’s What are you going through?, verified on the page, and one Weil per month. Page 462 rests on four scholarly citations. An attention line. Blocked by the cap: Simone Weil already stands three times in the year, in February, March and September, so this line cannot land at all. It should be retired rather than carried again.

retired.quote: Travel is in my opinion a very profitable exercise; the soul is there continually employed in observing new and unknown things, and I do not know, as I have often said a better school wherein to model life than by incessantly exposing to it the diversity of so many other lives, fancies, and usances, and by making it relish a perpetual variety of forms of human nature.
retired.source: Michel de Montaigne, Essays, Book III, ch. 9, Of Vanity (trans. Charles Cotton, revised by W. Carew Hazlitt, 1877)
retired.note: Verified. Another Montaigne is already held for May, so this goes on to the month of clear seeing. Blocked by the cap as of October: Montaigne now stands three times in the year, in May, June and October, so this second Montaigne line cannot land. It should be retired rather than carried again.

retired.source: Mark Twain, The Innocents Abroad, Conclusion (American Publishing Company, 1869)
